title: How Long Would You Last in Every Era of History?
idea: How long a modern person would survive if dropped into eight eras of history
question: Which era would you choose to live in for one year?

scenes.narration: Imagine you're pulled out of your bed tonight and dropped into the past. No phone, no money, no skills. Just you, in your pajamas.

claims.text: Time travel is a thought experiment
claims.source: Narrative device

scenes.narration: The question is simple: how long would you last? We'll go through eight eras, from the Ice Age to today, and rate each one.
A few rules. You get local clothes, and you magically understand the language. Everything else, you have to figure out yourself.
And fair warning: some of these levels end very quickly. Let's go.
Level one. Twenty thousand years ago, at the peak of the last Ice Age. Huge ice sheets cover much of the north.

claims.text: The Last Glacial Maximum was roughly 26,000-19,000 years ago
claims.source: Clark et al., 'The Last Glacial Maximum', Science 325 (2009)

scenes.narration: Scientists estimate the whole planet was around six degrees Celsius colder on average. In Europe, winters were brutal.

claims.text: Global mean temperature at the LGM was about 6°C below pre-industrial
claims.source: Tierney et al., 'Glacial cooling and climate sensitivity', Nature 584 (2020)

scenes.narration: Your first problem isn't the mammoths. It's the cold. In freezing, wet conditions, hypothermia can kill an unprotected person within hours.

claims.text: Hypothermia can become life-threatening within hours in cold, wet exposure
claims.source: UK NHS, 'Hypothermia'; US CDC, 'Hypothermia'

scenes.narration: To survive, you'd need fire, fur clothing, and a group. Ice Age people lived in small bands, hunting reindeer, horses and mammoths together.

claims.text: Upper Palaeolithic people lived in small hunter-gatherer bands hunting large game
claims.source: Mark Nathan Cohen, Health and the Rise of Civilization (1989)

scenes.narration: Here's the surprise: if they took you in, life wasn't all misery. Many hunter-gatherers were tall, strong and well fed, with plenty of free time.

claims.text: Skeletal evidence suggests many pre-agricultural foragers were relatively tall and well nourished
claims.source: Mark Nathan Cohen, Health and the Rise of Civilization (1989)

scenes.narration: Food is mostly meat and fat, plus fish, roots and berries when the season allows. Bone marrow was a prized treat.

claims.text: Ice Age diets in cold regions relied heavily on animal foods, supplemented by plants and fish
claims.source: Mark Nathan Cohen, Health and the Rise of Civilization (1989)

scenes.narration: Some groups even built huts out of mammoth bones. In Ukraine, archaeologists found shelters made from the bones of dozens of mammoths.

claims.text: Mammoth-bone dwellings are known from sites such as Mezhyrich, Ukraine
claims.source: Pidoplichko / Soffer — mammoth-bone dwellings at Mezhyrich, Ukraine (c. 15,000 years ago)

scenes.narration: And one of the most important inventions of the age? The sewing needle, made of bone. It let people make tight, warm clothes.

overlays.text: Eyed bone needles appear in the Upper Palaeolithic, enabling fitted clothing.
overlays.source: d'Errico et al., 'The origin and evolution of sewing technologies in Eurasia and North America' (2018)

claims.text: Eyed bone needles appear in the Upper Palaeolithic
claims.source: d'Errico et al., 'The origin and evolution of sewing technologies in Eurasia and North America' (2018)

scenes.narration: And you're not at the top of the food chain yet. Cave lions, wolves and cave bears shared this world with you.

claims.text: Ice Age Europe had cave lions, wolves and cave bears
claims.source: Stuart & Lister, Pleistocene megafauna of Europe (cave lions, wolves, bears)

scenes.narration: But you don't know how to hunt, track or make a spear. Alone, you'd last days. With a friendly band, maybe years.
Level two. Egypt, around twenty-five sixty B.C. The Great Pyramid of Giza is going up, and you've just been put on a work crew.

claims.text: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built c. 2560 BC (reign of Khufu)
claims.source: Ancient Egypt Research Associates (Mark Lehner) — Giza workers' town

scenes.narration: Forget the movies. The builders were most likely not slaves, but paid workers, many of them farmers doing a rotation.

overlays.text: Myth: "the pyramids were built by slaves"

claims.text: Archaeology at Giza indicates the pyramid builders were organized, paid and fed laborers, not slaves
claims.source: Ancient Egypt Research Associates (Mark Lehner) — Giza workers' town; Zahi Hawass, excavations of the pyramid builders' tombs at Giza

scenes.narration: And you'd be fed. Archaeologists found their town, with bakeries and breweries. The pay was bread and beer.

claims.text: The workers' town at Giza had bakeries and breweries; rations included bread and beer
claims.source: Ancient Egypt Research Associates (Mark Lehner) — Giza workers' town

scenes.narration: Even medical care. Skeletons from the workers' cemetery show broken bones that were set and healed.

overlays.text: Builders' tombs at Giza show healed fractures and even signs of surgery.
overlays.source: Zahi Hawass, excavations of the pyramid builders' tombs at Giza

claims.text: Skeletons of Giza workers show healed fractures, indicating medical care
claims.source: Zahi Hawass, excavations of the pyramid builders' tombs at Giza

scenes.narration: The workers were organized into gangs with team names. Graffiti left inside the pyramids include names like Friends of Khufu.

claims.text: Work-gang names such as 'Friends of Khufu' appear in graffiti at Giza
claims.source: AERA / Mark Lehner — work-gang names ('Friends of Khufu', 'Drunkards of Menkaure')

scenes.narration: At the next pyramid, one gang called itself the Drunkards of Menkaure. Which tells you something about the beer ration.

claims.text: A gang name 'Drunkards of Menkaure' is attested
claims.source: AERA / Mark Lehner — work-gang names ('Friends of Khufu', 'Drunkards of Menkaure')

scenes.narration: And about a thousand years later, at another royal work site, we have attendance records with excuses for skipping work.

claims.text: A Deir el-Medina absence register lists reasons such as brewing beer, scorpion stings and eye trouble
claims.source: British Museum EA 5634 — absence register from Deir el-Medina (c. 1250 BC)

scenes.narration: The danger is the work itself: dragging blocks of over two tons, in the heat, all day. Backs, knees and fingers paid the price.

claims.text: Most Great Pyramid blocks average around 2.5 tonnes
claims.source: Ancient Egypt Research Associates (Mark Lehner) — Giza workers' town

scenes.narration: Verdict: tough, but you'd probably survive for years. Level two is one of the safest on this list.
Level three. The year 793. You wake up on a Viking longship heading for the monastery of Lindisfarne in England.

claims.text: The Viking raid on Lindisfarne in 793 is often taken as the start of the Viking Age
claims.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, entry for 793 (Lindisfarne)

scenes.narration: The raid shocked Europe. The scholar Alcuin wrote that never before had such terror appeared in Britain.

overlays.text: Never before has such terror appeared in Britain…

claims.text: Alcuin wrote of the Lindisfarne raid's unprecedented terror
claims.source: Alcuin of York, letter to King Æthelred of Northumbria (793)

scenes.narration: First problem: the ship. It's open to the sky. No cabin, no roof. You sleep on deck, in the rain, wrapped in a wool blanket.

claims.text: Viking longships were open boats without enclosed cabins
claims.source: Viking Ship Museum, Roskilde (Skuldelev ships)

scenes.narration: Second surprise: your crewmates are cleaner than you expected. Vikings carried combs, tweezers and even little ear-cleaning spoons.

overlays.text: Combs are among the most common Viking-age finds.
overlays.source: National Museum of Denmark, 'Viking hygiene' (combs, tweezers, ear spoons)

claims.text: Viking-age finds include many combs, tweezers and ear spoons
claims.source: National Museum of Denmark, 'Viking hygiene' (combs, tweezers, ear spoons)

scenes.narration: And sorry to disappoint you: no horned helmets. That's a nineteenth-century costume idea. Real Viking helmets were plain iron caps.

claims.text: No horned helmets are known from the Viking Age; the image comes from 19th-century art and opera
claims.source: National Museum of Denmark — no Viking-age horned helmets (Gjermundbu helmet)

scenes.narration: Food on board: dried fish, salted meat, hard bread, and water or sour milk. For days at a time.

claims.text: Viking voyage provisions included dried fish, salted meat and bread
claims.source: Viking Ship Museum, Roskilde (Skuldelev ships)

scenes.narration: Then the raid itself. If you hang back with the ships, you might be fine. If you're in the front line, with no training, you're in serious trouble.
Verdict: a few weeks, maybe a season, depending on how good you are at hiding behind a shield.
Quick bonus level: ancient Rome, around the year one hundred. If you saw our Roman video, you already know the deal.
Work ends around lunch, the baths are cheap, and there's free grain if you're a citizen. Pretty good so far.

claims.text: Roman citizens received grain distributions; public baths were cheap
claims.source: Mary Beard, SPQR (2015); Juvenal, Satire 3

scenes.narration: The catch: fires, collapsing apartment blocks, and the noise. Verdict: years, as long as you avoid the top floor.

claims.text: Fires and building collapses were common hazards in Rome
claims.source: Mary Beard, SPQR (2015); Juvenal, Satire 3

scenes.narration: Level four. England, summer 1348. If you watched our medieval peasant video, you know exactly what's coming.
The Black Death. Somewhere between a third and a half of the population, possibly more, is about to die.

overlays.caption: 3 to 5 out of every 10 people died

claims.text: Black Death mortality in England is estimated at a third to a half or more
claims.source: Rosemary Horrox (ed.), The Black Death (Manchester University Press, 1994); Ole J. Benedictow, The Black Death 1346-1353 (Boydell, 2004)

scenes.narration: Your advantage? You know about germs. Avoid fleas and rats, don't crowd around the sick, and leave the city if you can.
People who could afford it did exactly that. In Florence, the writer Boccaccio described the rich fleeing to their country villas.

claims.text: Boccaccio describes people fleeing plague-stricken Florence for the countryside
claims.source: Giovanni Boccaccio, The Decameron (introduction, 1348-53)

scenes.narration: Within a few decades, cities started inventing quarantine: forty days of isolation for ships and travelers.

claims.text: Quarantine measures emerged in the late 14th century (Ragusa 1377; later 40-day 'quaranta giorni')
claims.source: Gensini et al., 'The concept of quarantine in history' (J. Infection, 2004)

scenes.narration: Your disadvantage? Everyone thinks you're very strange, and there's no cure. Verdict: honestly, a coin flip.
Level five. The Caribbean, around 1718, the Golden Age of Piracy. You've just signed on to a pirate crew.

claims.text: The 'Golden Age of Piracy' peaked c. 1715-1725
claims.source: Marcus Rediker, Villains of All Nations: Atlantic Pirates in the Golden Age (2004)

scenes.narration: Surprisingly, pirate ships were democratic. Crews voted for their captain and signed written rules, called articles.

claims.text: Pirate crews elected captains and agreed written articles (e.g., Bartholomew Roberts' articles)
claims.source: Captain Charles Johnson, A General History of the Pyrates (1724) — Bartholomew Roberts' articles; Marcus Rediker, Villains of All Nations: Atlantic Pirates in the Golden Age (2004)

scenes.narration: There was even compensation for injuries. Lose a leg in battle, and the crew paid you from the common fund.

claims.text: Pirate articles specified compensation for lost limbs
claims.source: Captain Charles Johnson, A General History of the Pyrates (1724) — Bartholomew Roberts' articles

scenes.narration: But the real killer at sea wasn't cannon fire. It was disease. Scurvy, from a lack of vitamin C, and tropical fevers.

overlays.text: Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) and fevers killed far more sailors than combat.
overlays.source: James Lind, A Treatise of the Scurvy (1753); NHS, 'Scurvy'

claims.text: Disease, including scurvy, killed more sailors than combat in the age of sail
claims.source: James Lind, A Treatise of the Scurvy (1753); NHS, 'Scurvy'

scenes.narration: The food? Hard ship's biscuit, often with weevils, salted meat, and whatever you could steal. Fresh fruit was gold.

claims.text: Shipboard diets relied on hardtack and salted meat; biscuits often had weevils
claims.source: James Lind, A Treatise of the Scurvy (1753); NHS, 'Scurvy'

scenes.narration: Walking the plank? Mostly a myth. Pirates had nastier punishments, like marooning: being left on a tiny island with a pistol and some water.

overlays.text: Walking the plank: very rarely, if ever, recorded

claims.text: Walking the plank is rarely attested; marooning was a recorded pirate punishment
claims.source: Rediker (2004); David Cordingly, Under the Black Flag (1995); Captain Charles Johnson, A General History of the Pyrates (1724) — Bartholomew Roberts' articles

scenes.narration: Even the most famous pirate of all, Blackbeard, lasted only about two years before he was killed in battle in 1718.

claims.text: Blackbeard's piracy lasted c. 1716-1718; he was killed at Ocracoke in November 1718
claims.source: North Carolina Dept. of Natural and Cultural Resources — Blackbeard killed at Ocracoke, 22 Nov 1718

scenes.narration: And the navy was hunting pirates down. Historians estimate most pirate careers lasted only a year or two.

claims.text: Most pirates' careers were short, typically one to two years
claims.source: Marcus Rediker, Villains of All Nations: Atlantic Pirates in the Golden Age (2004)

scenes.narration: Verdict: if you pack limes, you could last a year or two. Which, for a pirate, is a decent career.

claims.text: Citrus prevents scurvy (Lind's trial, 1747)
claims.source: James Lind, A Treatise of the Scurvy (1753); NHS, 'Scurvy'

scenes.narration: Level six. Manchester, England, the 1830s. The world's first great factory city, and you've just got a job in a cotton mill.

claims.text: Manchester was the leading cotton-mill city of the Industrial Revolution
claims.source: Edwin Chadwick, Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population (1842)

scenes.narration: Shifts of twelve hours or more, six days a week. The machines are deafening, the air is full of cotton dust.

claims.text: Early factory shifts commonly ran 12+ hours, six days a week
claims.source: UK Parliament, 'The 1833 Factory Act'

scenes.narration: And children worked too. A new law in 1833 banned kids under nine from textile mills, which tells you how common it was before.

overlays.text: 1833 Factory Act: no children under 9 in textile mills; ages 9-13 limited to 9 hours a day.

claims.text: The 1833 Factory Act banned under-9s from textile mills and limited 9-13 year olds' hours
claims.source: UK Parliament, 'The 1833 Factory Act'

scenes.narration: And time itself becomes your boss. Be a few minutes late and you're fined part of your wages. Some factories locked the gates.

claims.text: Factory discipline imposed fines for lateness
claims.source: E. P. Thompson, 'Time, Work-Discipline and Industrial Capitalism' (1967)

scenes.narration: Dinner: bread, potatoes, maybe a little bacon, and lots of sweet tea. Cheap calories to keep you standing.

claims.text: Working-class diets relied on bread, potatoes and sweetened tea
claims.source: Edwin Chadwick, Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population (1842)

scenes.narration: Home is a crowded, damp room, with shared toilets and dirty water. Cholera swept through these cities.

claims.text: Cholera epidemics struck British industrial cities in the 1830s-1840s
claims.source: Edwin Chadwick, Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population (1842)

scenes.narration: The machines had no guards. Children crawled underneath running looms to sweep up cotton, and accidents were common.

overlays.text: "scavengers": children who cleaned under working machines

claims.text: Child 'scavengers' cleaned beneath moving machinery in cotton mills
claims.source: UK Parliament, 'The 1833 Factory Act'

scenes.narration: A government report in 1842 found that the average age at death for laborers in Manchester was just seventeen. Mostly because so many children died.

overlays.caption: average age at death, Manchester laborers (1842)

claims.text: Chadwick's 1842 report gave an average age at death of 17 for Manchester labourers' families
claims.source: Edwin Chadwick, Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population (1842)

scenes.narration: As an adult, though, you'd probably survive. Verdict: years, but long, grey, exhausting ones.
Level seven. France, July 1916. You're a British soldier at the Battle of the Somme.

claims.text: The Battle of the Somme began on 1 July 1916
claims.source: Imperial War Museums, 'The first day of the Somme'

scenes.chapter: Level 7: The Trenches of World War One

scenes.narration: On the very first day, the British army suffered over fifty-seven thousand casualties, including about nineteen thousand dead. The worst day in its history.

claims.text: The British suffered 57,470 casualties, including 19,240 killed, on 1 July 1916
claims.source: Imperial War Museums, 'The first day of the Somme'

scenes.narration: Daily life was mud, rats, lice, and trench foot from standing in cold water for days.

claims.text: Trench life involved rats, lice and trench foot
claims.source: Imperial War Museums, 'What life was like in the trenches of WW1'

scenes.narration: But here's something most people don't know: soldiers didn't live in the front line all the time. They rotated, often spending only days at a time there.

claims.text: Units rotated between front line, support, reserve and rest
claims.source: Imperial War Museums, 'What life was like in the trenches of WW1'

scenes.narration: Food was monotonous: canned corned beef, called bully beef, rock-hard biscuits, and endless tea.

claims.text: British rations included bully beef, biscuits and tea
claims.source: Imperial War Museums — British soldiers' rations (bully beef, biscuits, tea)

scenes.narration: But the mail always came. Around two billion letters traveled between Britain and the front during the war.

overlays.caption: letters to and from the front

claims.text: Around 2 billion letters were sent between Britain and the front
claims.source: Imperial War Museums — around 2 billion letters were sent to and from the front

scenes.narration: Overall, roughly one in eight British soldiers who served was killed. Terrible odds, but most men came home.

overlays.caption: ≈ 1 in 8 British soldiers who served died

claims.text: About 12% of British soldiers who served in WW1 were killed
claims.source: Imperial War Museums / CWGC — roughly 1 in 8 British soldiers who served in WW1 died

scenes.narration: Verdict: with no training, on the first day of the Somme? Possibly minutes. Across the whole war, you'd more likely make it.
And finally, level eight. You wake up back in your own bed. Today.
Global life expectancy today is around seventy-three years. For almost all of history, it was less than half of that.

claims.text: Global life expectancy is about 73 years
claims.source: World Health Organization, World Health Statistics (global life expectancy ~73 years); UN World Population Prospects 2024

claims.text: Historic life expectancy at birth was typically around 30, mainly due to child mortality
claims.source: Mark Nathan Cohen, Health and the Rise of Civilization (1989)

scenes.narration: Verdict for level eight: decades. You're living in the safest era in human history, even on a bad day.
So, final ranking. The deadliest levels: the Ice Age alone, and the trenches on day one. The safest past era? Surprisingly, the pyramid site.
And notice the pattern. In almost every era, the biggest killer wasn't war or monsters. It was disease and cold, the boring stuff.

claims.text: Infectious disease was the leading cause of death through most of history
claims.source: Mark Nathan Cohen, Health and the Rise of Civilization (1989)

scenes.narration: So the next time you complain about your commute, remember: you could be dragging a two-ton block in the desert, or eating weevil biscuits on a pirate ship.
Modern life has its problems. But in terms of pure survival, we've never had it better.
Now, which level would you choose to live in for a year? Tell me in the comments. My vote is the pyramids, purely for the free beer.
And if you enjoyed this, subscribe for more stickman history. See you in the next era.

metadata.title: How Long Would You Last in Every Era of History?
metadata.description_intro:
You're pulled out of bed and dropped into the past — no phone, no money, no skills. How long would you last? Eight levels, from the Ice Age to today: a pyramid building site, a Viking raid, the Black Death, a pirate ship, a Victorian cotton mill and the trenches of the Somme — each one rated with a survival verdict.

A stickman history ranking with real facts and sources.
metadata.pinned_comment: Which era would you pick to live in for one year? 🤔 I'm going pyramids — free bread AND beer. 👇
